html:
The Concho, called Yoli on this map, were a people of the Conchos River basin in what is now Chihuahua, northern Mexico. They lived in villages along the rivers, growing maize, beans and squash where water allowed, and hunting and gathering in the desert beyond. The Spanish named them after the river.

Spanish silver miners and missionaries pushed into their land from the 1560s, after strikes at Santa Bárbara and later Parral, on the northern frontier of New Spain. The Concho were drafted to work in the mines, rose in revolts in the 1600s and suffered epidemics and slave raids. By the later 1700s they had merged into the Spanish-speaking rural population. Their neighbours included the Rarámuri to the west, the Toboso to the east and the Jumano to the north.
